Johann Forster
yō'hān for'ster
n. (Johann Forster, 1496–1558, Hebraist of Wittenberg and lexicographer)
German Johann, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Forster, a forester, keeper of a wood.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Johann Forster taught Hebrew at Wittenberg and gave the Reformation one of its most useful and least celebrated tools. He studied under Reuchlin, joined Luther's Bible revision committee, and spent the better part of thirty years on a Hebrew dictionary built on a principle that was itself a confession: the sense of a Hebrew word is to be gathered from the way Scripture uses it, not received from the rabbinic commentators as a fixed gloss. His Dictionarium Hebraicum Novum appeared in 1557, the year before he died. Whatever its lapses — and a first attempt of that size has many — the method was sound and it was the method the whole Protestant translating enterprise would adopt. A man who makes a dictionary is doing for others what Ezra's Levites did for the assembly at the water gate: putting the text within reach of a people who cannot read it in the original. “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines lexicon as a dictionary or word-book, and Hebraist as one versed in the Hebrew language.

expand to see more

LEX'ICON, n. A dictionary; a vocabulary or book containing an alphabetical arrangement of the words in a language, with the definition of each.

HE'BRAIST, n. One versed in the Hebrew language.

RAD'ICAL, a. In philology, pertaining to the root; original; underived.

IN'TERPRET, v. To explain the meaning of words to a person who does not understand them.

Key Scripture

Neh 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

2Ti 2:15 — "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth."

Psa 119:130 — "The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple."

Act 8:30 — "And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?"

Modern Corruption

The Wittenberg Hebraist who built a dictionary out of Scripture's own usage.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern habit of treating lexical work as neutral apparatus, as though a dictionary carried no commitments. Forster's did, and he said so. To define a Hebrew word by the range of its scriptural occurrences rather than by an inherited rabbinic gloss is to confess that Scripture interprets Scripture, and that the believing church reads the Old Testament in the light of the whole canon rather than under a borrowed authority.

The principle to recover is that a word-book is a servant of the pulpit and the plough, not an ornament of the academy. The point of the labour is the man in Acts who was reading aloud and could not follow what he read, and the question Philip put to him: “Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30). The Levites at the water gate “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). A lexicon exists for that sentence or it exists for nothing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew parash (H6567), to make distinct, to declare; sekel (H7922), understanding, prudence.

Hebrew parash (H6567) — to separate, to make distinct, to declare; Nehemiah 8:8.

Hebrew biyn (H995) — to discern, to cause to understand; Nehemiah 8:8.

Hebrew pethach (H6608) — an opening, an entrance; Psalm 119:130.

Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, to divide rightly; 2 Timothy 2:15.

Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know, to perceive, to understand; Acts 8:30.

Usage

"“gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — the office of a lexicon."

"“rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) — the Dictionarium Hebraicum Novum, 1557."

"“Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30) — why a Hebraist works thirty years."
